newsitem.title: ITALY: EU to discuss Alitalia plan by end-March.
newsitem.headline: EU to discuss Alitalia plan by end-March.

text.p: The EU will examine a rescue plan for debt-laden Italian flag carrier Alitalia by the end of this month to decide whether it constitutes unfair state aid, European Transport Commissioner Neil Kinnock said on Tuesday.
Kinnock told reporters after talks with Transport Minister Claudio Burlando that a report on the plan being drawn up by consultants Ernst and Young would be ready within the month.
He said the commission would then examine whether the Alitalia recapitalisation could be considered a market operation and not unfair state aid.

At stake for Alitalia is a request for Commission clearance, with as few conditions as possible, for a package of cash payments, share sales and pension subsidies worth nearly 3.5 trillion lire ($2 billion) in the run-up to the year 2000.

Dutch Transport Minister Annemarie Jorritsma, whose country holds the rotating presidency of the European Union and Alitalia managing director Domenico Cempella, attended the meeting and Kinnock also met Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi.
"We went into the merits and the details but it's too soon to draw conclusions and make forecasts," Burlando said.
"The European authorities would like to finish everything in March, before the liberalisation of the sector enters into force on April 1.
"In the next few weeks, there could be fresh meetings with the managers of Alitalia, with the government and with (state holding company) Iri. Then they will decide," he said.

Alitalia is heading for its ninth consecutive year in the red. Ciampi said last month that he expected the airline to post 1996 losses of around 1.3 trillion lire. That is largely because of restructuring costs of some 800 million lire.
Alitalia management was locked in bitter conflict with unions for more than a year over plans to slash hefty personnel costs and boost productivity.

A truce was finally called last June when labour leaders agreed to a rescue package which allowed for 20-30 percent of the group's shares to be reserved for employees after the firm's recapitalisation and privatisation.
Under the terms of the rescue plan, the airline called for a three trillion lire capital increase, with the government promising to provide much of the new cash.
In the meantime Alitalia has vowed to push ahead with its 38-point restructuring plan, which envisages staff numbers falling to 13,000 by the year 2000 from more than 16,000 now. ($1=1,705 lire).
